title: Gavaskar Questions India's Fitness Approach as Injury Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Former India captain says recurring hamstring injuries point to flawed training methods, argues being match fit matters more than being gym fit.
body:
• Gavaskar identifies recurring hamstring injuries across the Indian squad as evidence of flawed training methods, saying blame is unfairly directed at BCCI Centre of Excellence physios
  • Former captain questions biomechanics protocols that restrict bowlers to fewer deliveries in nets than they face in matches
  • Argues being "match fit" through playing cricket matters more than being "gym fit," echoing concerns raised by captain Shubman Gill after India's 1-2 ODI series loss to England
  • Six senior players — Bumrah, Sudharsan, Sundar, Pandya, Nitish Kumar Reddy, and Harshit Rana — currently sidelined with fitness issues as India play Tests against Sri Lanka

Sunil Gavaskar has weighed in on India's worsening injury crisis, questioning the team's training methods and defending the BCCI's Centre of Excellence against what he called misplaced blame. Writing in his Mid-Day column, the former India captain pointed to the pattern of hamstring injuries plaguing the squad and suggested the root cause lies in how players prepare, not in rehabilitation facilities.

India are currently without six senior players across formats. Jasprit Bumrah is dealing with left knee swelling and fluid retention sustained during the ODI series in England. B Sai Sudharsan has a big toe injury. Nitish Kumar Reddy and Harshit Rana are sidelined with hamstring problems. Washington Sundar has a quadriceps issue. And Hardik Pandya picked up a quadriceps strain while undergoing rehab at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence for a separate back injury.

The Blame Game

Gavaskar took direct aim at what he sees as scapegoating the CoE's medical staff for injuries that originate elsewhere.

"While Bumrah has a knee injury, it is seen that most Indian players suffer from hamstring injuries. Clearly, there's something wrong with their training, and that's why these recurring hamstring injuries. These injuries happen when they are playing for India, but unfortunately, the blame is put on the physios at the BCCI centre of excellence."

— Sunil Gavaskar, Mid-Day column

His comments come just a week after VVS Laxman, head of the Centre of Excellence, publicly defended the facility. Laxman pushed back against the perception that the CoE is merely a rehabilitation centre, saying it has "bigger roles to play in helping cricketers achieve excellence." He rejected the notion that blame should be assigned when injuries occur, stating, "We don't use the term blame — then we will be trying to find scapegoats."

Questioning Modern Biomechanics

Gavaskar reserved particular criticism for the biomechanics-driven approach to managing fast bowlers' workloads, which he called "a questionable practice."

"The so-called biomechanics, where a bowler can bowl only so many deliveries in the practice nets, is a questionable practice. Even in the IPL, it is learnt that some of the overseas physios don't allow the bowlers to bowl more than 20 balls in the nets. If in the match you will be bowling 24 balls, that is, if you don't bowl no-balls and wides, then how is bowling a lesser number in the nets going to help?"

— Sunil Gavaskar, Mid-Day column

The 76-year-old also made the broader argument that modern gym-based fitness routines may be doing more harm than good for cricketers. "It's an issue that needs a good, hard look at why these injuries are happening again and again. It is more important to be match fit than gym fit. But then, maybe I am from a generation that had different ideas on fitness," Gavaskar wrote.

Captain's Frustration

Gavaskar's critique follows captain Shubman Gill's pointed remarks after India's 1-2 ODI series defeat to England in July. Gill noted that five players from the original squad were unavailable by the series decider at Lord's. "If a player is missing after every match due to injury, somewhere we are missing a trick," Gill said. "Keeping the World Cup in mind, we have to play eleven matches in a row. And here the players are unable to finish a series of two or three matches."

A subsequent report in the Times of India revealed that injured players who do not recover at the CoE in Bengaluru "are largely left to their own devices," with little communication from the BCCI about their rehabilitation progress. The CoE's sports science team has been without a permanent head since physiotherapist Nitin Patel's departure in early 2025, and the facility has struggled to fill the Head of Sports Science and Medicine position.

A Familiar Debate for Diaspora Fans

For millions of Indian cricket fans watching from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, the injury debate carries an added dimension. India's depleted squads on overseas tours — where diaspora communities buy tickets and follow the action closely — have been a recurring disappointment. The ODI series loss in England, played across venues like Edgbaston, Cardiff, and Lord's where large South Asian crowds turn out, underscored the problem: India's best XI rarely takes the field together abroad.

What's Next

India's first Test against Sri Lanka is underway in Galle, where Devdutt Padikkal scored an unbeaten 131 on Day 1 after KL Rahul retired hurt with cramps — another reminder of fitness concerns within the squad. Both Bumrah and Sudharsan were named in the Test squad on a subject-to-fitness basis but were ultimately not cleared to play.

The broader question — whether India's approach to sports science is preparing players for the demands of international cricket or leaving them vulnerable — will likely dominate discussion through the 2027 World Cup cycle. As Laxman noted, the CoE has introduced the Bronco fitness test as an alternative to the Yo-Yo test for players on tour, but systemic changes to training philosophy may take longer to filter through.
